text: Every circuit you'll ever build in Qiskit, no matter how advanced, starts from the same object: QuantumCircuit. It's the blueprint — a container that records which qubits exist, which classical bits exist, and the ordered sequence of operations you apply to them, before anything is ever simulated or run.

The fastest way to get a working circuit is to pass QuantumCircuit the number of qubits you want, and optionally the number of classical bits. The qubits are unnamed and addressed only by integer index, which is perfectly fine for small, throwaway circuits where you don't need descriptive labels.

Once circuits get larger, or combine multiple logical groups of qubits, addressing everything by bare integer gets confusing. QuantumRegister and ClassicalRegister let you name a group of bits instead. This produces a circuit functionally identical to QuantumCircuit(2, 2), but now the qubits carry a name in diagrams — which matters once a circuit combines, say, three data qubits and one separate ancilla qubit, since the names tell you at a glance which qubits are doing which job.

A QuantumCircuit object by itself is just data — a list of instructions. To actually see it as a diagram, call dot draw. The default call renders a text diagram directly in your terminal, no extra dependencies required. Passing 'mpl' instead renders a proper graphical circuit diagram using Matplotlib, which is usually what you want when presenting or debugging visually in a notebook.

A QuantumCircuit also exposes properties describing its own shape, independent of any simulation. num_qubits is simply how many qubits it was built with. depth counts the longest chain of sequentially-dependent operations — roughly how many layers of gates have to happen one after another. A freshly created circuit with no gates has a depth of exactly zero, since there's nothing sequential to count yet.
Next lesson puts something actually useful onto this blueprint: the core single-qubit gates — X, Y, Z, H, S, T — plus the parameterized rotation gates RX, RY, and RZ.
